readerTitle: Uniqlo's ¥1,900 fleece: when the price comes first
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Uniqlo/Fast Retailing, IKEA, Toyota의 원가기획) + 가상 적용 (목재 의자 제조사)
insight: 가격은 원가를 계산한 결과가 아니라, 먼저 정하고 사업 전체를 거기에 맞추는 설계 조건이 될 수 있다.
misconception: 가격은 원가에 마진을 더해 정하는 것이고, 지금 원가보다 낮은 가격은 처음부터 불가능하다.

sources.text: Fast Retailing, corporate history (1998 Harajuku store, ¥1,900 fleece, fleece unit sales 1998–2000)
Fast Retailing annual reports FY2001–FY2003 (sales and profit decline after the fleece boom)
IKEA, Democratic Design (starting product development from the price tag)
Cooper, R. & Slagmulder, R. (1997). Target Costing and Value Engineering. Productivity Press.
Fast Retailing / Uniqlo, HeatTech launch history (2003)

factChecks.note: 하라주쿠 점 개점 시기(1998년 11월)와 ¥1,900 플리스 캠페인은 Fast Retailing 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요.
플리스 판매량 약 200만 장(1998), 약 850만 장(1999), 약 2,600만 장(2000)은 회사 연혁에 자주 인용되는 수치입니다. 게시 전 공식 자료로 정확한 수치와 연도 기준(회계연도 여부)을 확인하세요.
당시 아웃도어 브랜드 플리스 가격은 구체적 수치 없이 '몇 배'로만 표현했습니다. 근거 자료(언론 기사 등)를 확인하고, 불확실하면 'much higher'로 완화하세요.
2001년 이후 붐이 식고 매출·이익이 2년가량 감소했다는 내용은 FY2002~FY2003 연차보고서로 확인하세요. 구체적 금액은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
생산 방식 설명(자체 기획·판매, 주로 중국의 협력 공장, 적은 디자인을 대량 생산)은 일반적으로 알려진 SPA 모델 설명입니다. 원단 대량 구매로 단가를 낮췄다는 부분은 정성적으로만 썼으니 자료로 확인하세요.
IKEA가 가격표부터 정하고 디자인한다는 설명, 원가기획이 Toyota 등 일본 제조사에서 발전했다는 설명은 공식 자료와 Cooper & Slagmulder(1997)로 확인하세요.
HeatTech 출시 연도(2003년)를 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도를 쓰지 않았습니다.
의자 사례 계산: 현재 원가 $50, 소매업체 희망 납품가 $45, 필요 마진 $8이면 목표 원가 $45 − $8 = $37.

cards.title: Uniqlo's ¥1,900 fleece
body: In November 1998, the Japanese clothing chain Uniqlo opened its first store in Tokyo's fashionable Harajuku district. The star item was a fleece jacket priced at ¥1,900.
At the time, fleece in Japan was mostly sold by outdoor brands, often for several times that price. Where Uniqlo's number came from is the interesting part.

image.label: Stacks of fleece jackets in many colors with a ¥1,900 tag
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 매장 선반에 여러 색의 같은 플리스 재킷이 무지개처럼 쌓여 있고, 가운데 큰 가격표 "¥1,900". 실제 Uniqlo 로고나 매장 간판은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you price your fleece?
body: It's 1998. You run a chain of casual clothing stores in Japan. Fleece is popular, but outdoor brands sell it at high prices.
Making and selling fleece the way the industry usually does would put your price close to theirs. How do you set yours?

options.text: Price it a little below the outdoor brands
options.feedback: You win some sales, but shoppers see a slightly cheaper version of the same thing. It doesn't change who buys fleece.

options.text: Add your usual markup to what it costs you today
options.feedback: Your margin is safe, but the price lands near everyone else's. Today's costs end up deciding your market for you.

options.text: Pick a price that would shock shoppers, then rebuild how it's made to hit it
options.feedback: The biggest upside, and what Uniqlo did. It only works if you can truly cut costs and sell in huge volume.

cards.title: A price that turned into a craze.
body: Uniqlo chose ¥1,900. According to the company's own history, fleece sales grew roughly thirteenfold in two years.
The fleece became the product that made Uniqlo a household name across Japan.

image.label: A price that turned into a craze.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Price-led costing
body: **Price-led costing**, often called *target costing*, flips the usual order. Cost-plus says: cost + markup = price. Price-led costing says: target price − the margin you need = the cost you must hit.
The price becomes a design requirement, like a size or a color. Designers, buyers and factories then work to fit inside it.

image.label: Two arrows: cost to price, and price to cost
image.brief: 두 줄 비교 인포그래픽. 위: "Cost + markup → Price" (회색). 아래: "Target price − margin → Cost to hit" (강조색). 아래 줄 화살표가 반대 방향임을 강조.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams do this when they pick a low monthly price small businesses will pay, then design the product so customers can sign up and get started without a salesperson. The price decides how much hand-holding the business can afford.

cards.title: Rebuilding the jacket around ¥1,900.
body: Uniqlo could only hit its price by changing how the fleece was made and sold:
list: **It ran the whole chain:** Uniqlo designed, ordered and sold its own clothes instead of buying from wholesalers
**Close factory partners:** it worked with a limited set of factories, mostly in China, and checked quality itself
**Few designs, many colors:** one simple fleece instead of many styles
**Huge orders:** big volumes lowered the cost per jacket
cards.callout: Volume made the price possible, and the price made the volume possible.
cards.softwareNote: The same loop shows up in digital products: a low price only works if the cost of serving each extra customer stays small as you grow.

cards.title: Others start with the price tag too.
body: IKEA describes a similar habit: product designers often begin with the price, then choose materials and flat-pack shapes to match.

Japanese manufacturers, notably carmakers like Toyota, are widely credited with turning target costing into a formal method. The common thread: the customer's price is fixed early, and everything inside the business bends around it.

image.label: A price tag drawn first, with a product sketched around it
image.brief: 설계 도면 위에 가격표가 먼저 그려져 있고, 그 주위로 의자와 자동차 스케치가 점선으로 맞춰 그려지는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A famous low price is hard to live with.
body: By 2001 the fleece craze was cooling. Uniqlo's sales and profits fell for the next couple of years, and many shoppers saw it as the cheap fleece shop.

Price-led costing needs big, steady demand to pay for the volume it's built on. Hits fade. And a famous low price sets what customers expect from you. Uniqlo responded with new fabric-driven products like HeatTech, not deeper discounts.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture maker.
body: You make wooden kitchen stools. Built your usual way, each costs $50, and you sell to shops at $70.
A large home-goods retailer says it could sell tens of thousands if your price to them were $45. What do you do?

options.text: Decline. $45 is below what a stool costs you
options.feedback: You protect your margin but treat today's cost as fixed. An order this size might pay for a cheaper way of making stools.

options.text: Counter at $60 and hope they meet you halfway
options.feedback: You might keep the deal, but you're still pricing from today's cost. The retailer is asking for a shelf price, not a negotiation.

options.text: Work backward: if you need $8 a stool, design one that costs $37, and commit only once prototypes prove it
options.feedback: Flat-pack legs, fewer parts and long runs might get you there. You take on design work and volume risk in exchange for a much bigger business.

cards.title: Sometimes the price should come first.
body: Cost-plus lets today's costs decide your price. Price-led costing asks what price would change customers' minds, then makes the business fit it.
**Try it today:** pick one product and name the price that would make customers say "I'll take two." List what would have to change for you to make money at that price.
